Count Integers Remaining After a Partial Prime Sieve

primePhi.Rd

Count the positive integers less than or equal to \(n\) that are not divisible by any of the first \(a\) primes. This is the partial-sieve function \(\Phi(n, a)\) used in combinatorial prime counting, not Euler's totient function.

Usage

primePhi(n, a, nThreads = NULL)

Arguments

n

A single nonnegative whole number, at most \(2^{53} - 1\).

a

A single nonnegative whole number, at most \(2^{53} - 1\). This is the number of initial primes to exclude, not a prime value or an upper bound on the excluded primes. For example, a = 3 excludes multiples of 2, 3, and 5. With a = 0, no primes are excluded.

nThreads

Requested number of threads. The default is NULL for serial execution. Requests are capped by the available hardware and the useful work in the calculation. Small or simple cases may use fewer threads. This argument is validated even when the result is immediate.

Details

Logical inputs FALSE and TRUE are converted to 0 and 1, respectively. The thread count must be positive, so nThreads = FALSE is not supported.

Mathematical definition

Write \(p_1 = 2, p_2 = 3, p_3 = 5, \ldots\) for the increasing sequence of primes. Then \(\Phi(n, a)\) counts integers \(m\) with \(1 \le m \le n\) for which none of \(p_1, \ldots, p_a\) divides \(m\). When \(a = 0\), the excluded set is empty. In particular, $$\Phi(n, 0) = n, \qquad \Phi(0, a) = 0.$$ For \(a \ge 1\), removing multiples of the next prime gives $$\Phi(n, a) = \Phi(n, a - 1) - \Phi(\lfloor n / p_a \rfloor, a - 1).$$ The subtracted term counts the multiples of \(p_a\) that survived removal of the preceding primes.

The integer 1 survives every partial sieve. Thus, when \(n > 0\), the answer is at least 1, and it is exactly 1 when \(a \ge \pi(n)\), where \(\pi(n)\) is the number of primes at most \(n\). Composite numbers can also survive: for example, primePhi(30, 2) includes 25 because neither 2 nor 3 divides it. This gives the ten survivors 1, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, 25, 29.

Euler's totient \(\phi(n)\) instead counts integers at most \(n\) that are coprime to \(n\) itself. For that function, see eulerPhiSieve.

Relation to prime counting

If \(a = \pi(\lfloor \sqrt n \rfloor)\) and \(n \ge 1\), every surviving integer other than 1 is a prime larger than the excluded primes. Legendre's formula is therefore $$\pi(n) = \Phi(n, a) + a - 1.$$ Smaller choices of \(a\) leave composite survivors. Meissel and Lehmer prime counting account for these using the correction terms exposed by semiPrimeCount and triPrimeCount. See primeCount for the corresponding formulas.

Note

The general calculation prepares prime and prime-count tables with storage proportional to \(\sqrt n\). Cases with \(a \le 6\) use small periodic tables instead of a full square-root table. Large values of \(a\) do not require preparing all of the first \(a\) primes merely to establish that the answer is 1.

The largest supported table limit is 94,906,265. Its dense prime-count table alone requires \(4(L + 1)\) bytes for limit \(L\), about 362 MiB at that maximum. Prime vectors, the shared Phi cache, temporary storage, and allocation overhead require additional memory. Workers within one call share the prepared tables; separate calls prepare their own tables. The numeric input range does not guarantee that every calculation is practical for the available resources.

Value

A single whole number giving \(\Phi(n, a)\). The result has type integer when it is at most .Machine$integer.max, and type double otherwise. The count is exact throughout the supported range.

Author

Joseph Wood

See also

primeCount, semiPrimeCount, triPrimeCount, eulerPhiSieve, primeSieve

Examples

## Remove multiples of the first two primes, 2 and 3
primePhi(30, 2)  ## 10
#> [1] 10

## No excluded primes; an empty interval; all primes through n excluded
primePhi(30, 0)   ## 30
#> [1] 30
primePhi(0, 2)    ## 0
#> [1] 0
primePhi(30, 100) ## 1
#> [1] 1

## Recover the prime count using Legendre's formula
n <- 1000
a <- primeCount(floor(sqrt(n)))
primePhi(n, a) + a - 1 == primeCount(n)
#> [1] TRUE
